arXiv:2607.04037v1 [cs.LG] 04 Jul 2026

Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation

Mohammad Sadegh Akhondzadeh Affiliation: University of Cologne Email: ms.akhondzadeh@gmail.com    Vijay Lingam Affiliation: AWS AI Email: vijaylingam0810@gmail.com    Atula Tejaswi Affiliation: UT Austin    Chanakya Ekbote Affiliation: MIT    Sujay Sanghavi Affiliation: UT Austin    Aleksandar Bojchevski Affiliation: University of Cologne
Abstract

On-policy distillation is a powerful way to transfer reasoning ability from a strong teacher to a smaller student: the student samples trajectories from its own policy, and the teacher provides dense token-level supervision on the states the student actually visits. However, this supervision is not always reliable: a teacher can assign high likelihood to plausible but incorrect solutions, or low likelihood to correct student solutions that follow different reasoning paths. Unconditionally distilling the teacher can therefore reinforce bad modes or erase useful student behavior. To address these limitations, we introduce RG-OPD: Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation that uses verifier feedback to decide when teacher logits should be trusted. RG-OPD bridges sparse verifier rewards and dense teacher logits, preserving token-level supervision while filtering misleading teacher signals. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, RG-OPD produces stronger distilled students, outperforming both vanilla reverse-KL distillation and the recent TSD-KD baseline. At 1K generation length, RG-OPD improves over reverse-KL by 2.9 points and over TSD-KD by 4.9 points; in the long-generation setting, it improves over the untuned student by 8.2 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/UoC-tail/RG-OPD.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) is an effective way to transfer reasoning ability from a strong teacher model to a smaller student. In OPD, the student samples trajectories from its own policy, and the teacher provides dense token-level supervision on the states the student actually visits (Agarwal et al., 2024). This makes OPD especially attractive for reasoning post-training: verifier rewards from RLVR provide only sparse trajectory-level feedback, while teacher logits provide a learning signal at every token. In its standard form, OPD applies this supervision unconditionally, treating the teacher as a reliable oracle for all rollouts. However, a teacher may assign high likelihood to a plausible but incorrect solution, or low likelihood to a correct student solution that follows a different reasoning path. Unconditional distillation can therefore reinforce incorrect modes or suppress useful student behaviors.

Based on these observations, we introduce RG-OPD: Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation, which addresses the following question: When does teacher supervision help rather than hurt during on-policy distillation? At each training step, the student samples trajectories on policy, a verifier assigns each trajectory a scalar reward or advantage, and a fixed teacher provides token-level distributions over the student’s sampled states. Instead of applying the distillation loss to every trajectory, RG-OPD keeps only trajectories for which the verifier reward and the teacher–student likelihood gap agree. For reward-positive trajectories, we distill only when the teacher assigns higher likelihood than the student; for reward-negative trajectories, we distill only when the teacher assigns lower likelihood than the student.

This simple gate preserves the main advantage of logit-level distillation: dense token-level supervision from a stronger model. At the same time, it avoids the central failure mode of unconditional distillation: treating the teacher as reliable even when its likelihoods conflict with observed correctness. Thus, RG-OPD provides a direct bridge between sparse verifier rewards and dense teacher logits. Unlike RLVR (Shao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Ekbote et al., 2025), it does not rely solely on terminal rewards; unlike standard on-policy distillation (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024), it does not assume the teacher is always correct; and unlike joint RL–KD objectives (Xu et al., 2025; Hübotter et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), it explicitly conditions each distillation update on trajectory-level reliability.

2 Related Work

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a practical post-training paradigm for reasoning tasks with automatically scored outputs (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). PPO, GRPO, and related variants optimize student-generated rollouts from sparse outcome rewards (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Ekbote et al., 2025), but terminal feedback provides limited token-level credit assignment, especially when correct samples are rare. Knowledge distillation offers a complementary signal by transferring dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher (Hinton et al., 2015); on-policy distillation further reduces exposure bias by querying the teacher on student-generated trajectories. GKD formalizes on-policy distillation for autoregressive language models, querying the teacher on student-generated outputs with divergences such as reverse KL or Jensen–Shannon divergence (Agarwal et al., 2024). TSD-KD builds on this student-centric perspective with preference-based and token-selective distillation (Kim and Baek, 2026). However, TSD-KD applies teacher supervision broadly and does not test whether the teacher is reliable on a given trajectory. Recent and concurrent work also combines verifier rewards with teacher-like supervision: KDRL adds teacher reverse-KL regularization to GRPO-style optimization (Xu et al., 2025); RL-aware distillation anchors the policy ratio to a mixture of the old student and teacher policies (Zhang et al., 2026); Self-Distilled RLVR uses a privileged variant of the same policy for token-level guidance (Yang et al., 2026); and related self-distillation methods derive dense guidance from privileged or feedback-conditioned student variants (Zhao et al., 2026; Hübotter et al., 2026). These methods show that dense teacher-like signals can improve reward-based reasoning post-training, but they either apply distillation as a broad auxiliary signal, modify the RL objective, or focus on self-distillation. In contrast, RG-OPD studies external-teacher on-policy distillation and gates each trajectory-level distillation update based on agreement between verifier reward and the teacher–student likelihood gap.

3 Reward-Gated On-Policy Distillation

On-policy distillation. We consider on-policy distillation of a student policy πθ\pi_{\theta} from a fixed teacher πT\pi_{T}. At each iteration, for each prompt xx, the student samples NN trajectories from its own policy: {y(i)}i=1N∼πθ(⋅|x)\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\,|\,x), and a verifier returns a scalar reward rir_{i} for each trajectory. For every sampled token yt(i)y_{t}^{(i)} we have access to three log-probabilities evaluated at the sampled action: the current student log⁡πθ​(yt(i)|st(i))\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}^{(i)}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}), the behavior policy at sampling time log⁡πθold​(yt(i)|st(i))\log\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{t}^{(i)}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}), and the teacher log⁡πT​(yt(i)|st(i))\log\pi_{T}(y_{t}^{(i)}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}). We follow (Hübotter et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026) and apply the top-k reverse-KL (Appendix A.2) distillation loss i.e. ℒKL(i)=∑tmt(i)KL(πθ(⋅|st(i))∥πT(⋅|st(i)))\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}^{(i)}\;=\;\sum_{t}m_{t}^{(i)}\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)})\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)})\right), where mt(i)m_{t}^{(i)} is the response mask. This loss is applied uniformly across sampled trajectories, regardless of whether the trajectory was successful and regardless of whether the teacher actually provides useful information at it.

When the teacher and the reward disagree. In the RLVR context, vanilla on-policy distillation can lead to two failure modes: (i) Teacher disagrees with a student success: the student samples a correct continuation that the teacher would have been unlikely to produce. Pulling the student toward the teacher in this case unlearns a behavior the reward signal certifies as good. (ii) Teacher endorses a student failure: The student samples a wrong trajectory to which the teacher also assigns high probability. Reverse-KL has nothing to push against here, the teacher’s mode coincides with the bad mode. A reward signal alone resolves neither case (it cannot tell the student what to do differently), and a teacher signal alone resolves neither (it has no information about correctness on a freshly sampled trajectory). The resolution is to use them jointly: the reward decides whether the trajectory is good, and the teacher–student likelihood gap decides whether the teacher is informative about the cause.

Reward-Teacher Likelihood Gate. For each sampled trajectory ii, define the trajectory-level teacher and student log-likelihoods evaluated on the sampled tokens,

LT(i)=∑tmt(i)​log⁡πT​(yt(i)|st(i)),LS(i)=∑tmt(i)​log⁡πθ​(yt(i)|st(i)),L_{T}^{(i)}\;=\;\sum_{t}m_{t}^{(i)}\log\pi_{T}\!\left(y_{t}^{(i)}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right),\qquad L_{S}^{(i)}\;=\;\sum_{t}m_{t}^{(i)}\log\pi_{\theta}\!\left(y_{t}^{(i)}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right), (1)

and let AiA_{i} denote the trajectory-level reward signal (we use the GRPO advantage of y(i)y^{(i)} in our experiments). We define the reward–teacher gate

gi=[(Ai>0∧LT(i)>LS(i)+δ)∨(Ai≤0∧LT(i)<LS(i)−δ)],g_{i}\;=\;\mathbbm{1}\!\left[\,{\color[rgb]{0.4141,0.6016,0.3047}\big(A_{i}>0\,\wedge\,L_{T}^{(i)}>L_{S}^{(i)}+\delta\big)}\;\vee\;{\color[rgb]{0.7695,0.2695,0.2109}\big(A_{i}\leq 0\,\wedge\,L_{T}^{(i)}<L_{S}^{(i)}-\delta\big)}\,\right], (2)

with an optional confidence margin δ≥0\delta\geq 0 (default δ=0\delta=0). The gated distillation loss is

ℒRG​-​OPD=∑igi∑tmt(i)KL(πθ(⋅|st(i))∥πT(⋅|st(i)))∑igi​∑tmt(i).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RG\text{-}OPD}}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{i}g_{i}\sum_{t}m_{t}^{(i)}\,\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)})\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)})\right)}{\sum_{i}g_{i}\sum_{t}m_{t}^{(i)}}. (3)

The student is updated only on trajectories for which the teacher gives a directionally useful signal relative to the observed reward; all other trajectories are dropped from the distillation loss. The same reverse-KL objective is used in both kept regimes; only the set of trajectories contributing to the loss changes.

4 Experiments

Following (Kim and Baek, 2026), we use Qwen2.5-1.5B/14B-Instruct models as the student-teacher pair and train on a subset of the UltraInteract (Yuan et al., 2024) for 3 epochs. We provide implementation details in Appendix A.

Results. In Table 1, we evaluate all methods with the default maximum generation length of 1024 tokens. RG-OPD achieves the best average score (46.94) among all distilled models, outperforming the vanilla Reverse-KL baseline (44.02) by 2.9 points and TSD-KD (42.03). Gains are consistent across math and coding tasks. An exception is IFEval, where TSD-KD achieves the best score (54.68) and RG-OPD scores 48.60. We attribute this to TSD-KD’s student-centric design: rather than enforcing the teacher distribution uniformly, it combines preference-based indirect feedback, token-selective distillation, and entropy regularization, which may better preserve the student’s instruction-following behavior while still providing teacher guidance.

As shown in Figure 2 [Center], distilled models tend to become more verbose over training, generating longer chains of thought on average. We therefore repeat the evaluation with a generous generation budget of 8096 tokens. With more room to reason, RG-OPD improves its average to 53.74, a 6.8-point gain over long-context Reverse-KL (50.90) and an 8.2-point improvement over the untuned student (45.59). The gains are especially pronounced on MATH, where RG-OPD reaches 52.60 vs. 49.80.

Training Dynamics. Figure 2 tracks three quantities over the course of RG-OPD training. Kept Token Fraction (left): the fraction of tokens admitted by the gate decreases over training, from roughly 0.9 to 0.7. This indicates that the teacher–student likelihood gap gradually shrinks, and fewer trajectories satisfy the alignment condition that triggers the gate. The gate therefore becomes more selective as training progresses, naturally reducing the distillation signal on trajectories where the teacher has little remaining information to offer. Response Length (center): the average number of generated tokens grows steadily throughout training; a consequence of imitating a teacher whose reasoning traces are more verbose. RG-OPD Loss (right): the gated reverse-KL loss decreases, confirming that the student is approaching the teacher’s distribution on the gated trajectories.

5 Conclusion

We present RG-OPD, an on-policy distillation method that conditions teacher supervision on the agreement between verifier feedback and the teacher–student likelihood gap. The key insight is that dense teacher logits and sparse verifier rewards answer different questions. The reward certifies whether a trajectory is good, while the likelihood gap reveals whether the teacher is directionally informative for the student. By applying distillation only when these two signals are aligned, RG-OPD avoids the two failure modes of unconditional distillation: (i) reinforcing bad modes that the teacher endorses, (ii) erasing correct student behaviors that the teacher would not have produced. Experimental results show that RG-OPD outperforms both reverse-KL distillation and the TSD-KD baseline. Our results support the view that the value of a teacher signal on any given trajectory depends on the reward, and that a simple scalar gate is sufficient to exploit this structure.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Setup

We adopt the setup from [10]; we distill a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct student from a frozen Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct teacher. The student is trained end-to-end with FSDP across 2 GPUs; the teacher is served via a dedicated vLLM endpoint (tensor-parallel =2=2). At each training step, the teacher receives the student’s rollouts and returns the top-KK log-probabilities at every position for KL distillation. Our training data is a subset of the UltraInteract [22]. We train for 3 epochs with AdamW (lr =×10−6=5\!\times\!10^{-6}, cosine schedule, 50-step warmup). Top-KK logit distillation uses K=50K=50 with tail correction ( Equation 4) as default. Our evaluations are performed on lm-eval-harness11 1 https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness, following [10].

Finally for the evaluation, we evaluate on 10 benchmarks spanning math (GSM8K [3], GSM-Plus [11], MATH [7], MMLU-Pro-Math [18] denoted as MPMath in our tables), code (MBPP [2]), knowledge (SciQ [19], MMLU-STEM [18]), reasoning (BBH [17], MuSR [16]), and instruction-following (IFEval [26]), using lm-evaluation-harness with vLLM as the inference backend. All models are evaluated with temperature=0.6 over 3 seeds.

A.2 Top-KK Reverse-KL Approximation.

Computing KL(πθ∥πT)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T}) naively requires storing the full vocabulary logits of both the student and the teacher simultaneously. To avoid this, similar to [9, 15], we use only the top-KK teacher logits indexed by the student’s top-KK tokens and approximate the full-vocabulary reverse-KL as a top-KK explicit sum plus a tail correction that aggregates the remaining probability mass into a single bucket:

KL(πθ(⋅|st(i))∥πT(⋅|st(i)))\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)})\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)})\right)
≈∑y^t∈topK​(πθ)πθ​(y^t|st(i))⋅log⁡πθ​(y^t|st(i))πT​(y^t|st(i))\displaystyle\approx{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}\sum_{\hat{y}_{t}\,\in\,\mathrm{top}_{K}(\pi_{\theta})}\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right)\cdot\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right)}{\pi_{T}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right)}}
+(1−∑y^t∈topK​(πθ)πθ(y^t|st(i)))⋅log1−∑y^t∈topK​(πθ)πθ​(y^t|st(i))1−∑y^t∈topK​(πθ)πT​(y^t|st(i)),\displaystyle\quad+{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.3516,0}\Bigl(1-\!\!\!\sum_{\hat{y}_{t}\,\in\,\mathrm{top}_{K}(\pi_{\theta})}\!\!\!\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right)\Bigr)\cdot\log\frac{1-\sum_{\hat{y}_{t}\,\in\,\mathrm{top}_{K}(\pi_{\theta})}\pi_{\theta}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right)}{1-\sum_{\hat{y}_{t}\,\in\,\mathrm{top}_{K}(\pi_{\theta})}\pi_{T}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\,|\,s_{t}^{(i)}\right)}}, (4)

where topK​(πθ)\mathrm{top}_{K}(\pi_{\theta}) denotes the KK tokens with highest probability under the current student πθ\pi_{\theta}. The blue term accumulates the per-token KL contribution over the top-KK support and carries the primary gradient signal for the student. The orange tail term handles the residual mass: it collapses all out-of-top-KK tokens into a single aggregate token then forms a binary KL between the student’s and teacher’s residual probabilities. The tail term also remains differentiable and gradients flow through it during backpropagation. Table 2 ablates the effect of KK and the tail correction. Removing the tail term (i.e., dropping the residual-mass bucket) degrades performance, confirming that the tail gradient is a non-trivial part of the learning signal even though its contribution to the total KL is small. Varying KK shows diminishing returns beyond a moderate value, indicating that the student’s probability mass is already well concentrated in the top-KK tokens.

Appendix B Additional Results

Likelihood-Based Tasks

We evaluate on tasks scored by log-likelihood ranking (SciQ, MMLU-STEM, MuSR, BBH), where the model assigns log-probabilities to a fixed set of answer choices and the highest-scoring option is selected as the prediction, following [10]. We note, however, that log-likelihood ranking is not the most natural evaluation protocol for instruction fine-tuned models. As shown in Table 3, RG-OPD does not consistently improve over the baseline under this protocol. These models are optimized to generate free-form responses and are not calibrated for pairwise answer scoring. This is evident from the teacher itself: despite being a 14B model that scores 80.01 on generation-based benchmarks, it achieves only 63.77 under likelihood-based evaluation and on SciQ, the 1.5B student baseline actually outscores the teacher (89.50 vs. 86.80). Finally, when we evaluate the models through text generation and extract the final answers, we observe that RG-OPD again outperforms the previous methods.
